title: Data structures and their costs
note: A data structure is a trade-off: it makes some operations cheap by making others expensive. Arrays give O(1) indexing, linked lists give O(1) insertion at a known node, hash tables give O(1) average lookup, balanced trees keep order with O(log n) operations, and heaps give fast access to the minimum or maximum.

read.title: Pick the structure for the question you ask most
text: Every data structure answers some questions quickly and others slowly, so the right choice depends on which operations your program performs most. An array stores items side by side in memory. That makes reading element i instant and plays well with CPU caches, but inserting at the front forces every element to shift. A linked list flips the trade: splicing in a node next to one you already hold is O(1), while finding the k-th node means walking from the head.

A hash table turns a key into an array index with a hash function. On average, lookups, inserts, and deletes are O(1). Two keys can land in the same bucket, a collision, which is handled by chaining or by probing for another slot. If many keys collide, operations degrade toward O(n), so tables resize when the load factor gets too high.

When you need order, use a tree. A balanced binary search tree such as a red-black tree supports search, insert, delete, and sorted traversal in O(log n). A binary heap is weaker but cheaper: it only promises that each parent beats its children, which is enough to read the minimum in O(1) and remove it in O(log n). That is exactly what a priority queue needs.

q.q: Why is inserting at the front of an array slow?
o: The hash function must be recomputed
Every element has to shift over
The array must be sorted first

q.q: What makes hash table operations degrade toward O(n)?
o: Many keys colliding in the same buckets

q.q: Why is a heap enough for a priority queue?
o: It keeps all keys fully sorted
It stores items side by side for cache speed
Its parent-beats-children rule exposes the minimum cheaply
